About 385 workers were locked out after the union rejected the company's latest contract offer, Teamsters Local 877 said in a social media post on Monday. Phillips 66's proposal included concessions on wages, healthcare and safety protections, the union said. Union representatives did not immediately respond to Reuters' request for comment. The Bayway refinery is capable of processing about 275,000 barrels per day of crude oil. The facility produces a high percentage of transportation fuels including gasoline and diesel for the region. The labor dispute follows a [USN:L1N4051A8 TEXT:"7-month long lockout"] at BP's (BP.L) Whiting refinery, the largest in the Midwest.

item.title: Dolphins release K Riley Patterson, sign Zane Gonzalez
item.description: The Miami Dolphins released kicker Riley Patterson on Tuesday and signed Zane Gonzalez to the practice squad as his expected replacement.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The Miami Dolphins released kicker Riley Patterson on Tuesday and signed Zane Gonzalez to the practice squad as his expected replacement. The Dolphins (0-5) also signed edge Rodney McGraw to the active roster from the practice squad and waived cornerback Storm Duck and edge Andre Jones Jr. Gonzalez worked out for Miami along with seven-time Pro Bowl kicker Justin Tucker, NFL insider Jordan Schultz reported earlier Tuesday. Gonzalez, 31, first signed with Miami as a free agent on March 12, was placed on injured reserve on Aug. 10 and waived on Aug. 19 due to injury. He was 19 of 22 (86.4%) on field-goal attempts with a long of 56, and made 17 of 18 extra-point attempts in nine games with the Atlanta Falcons last season. Gonzalez is 115 of 142 (81.0%) on field goals and 163 of 171 (95.3%) on extra points in 79 regular-season games for five teams since 2017. He did not appear in an NFL game from 2022-23. Patterson, 27, was in his second season with the Dolphins. After missing only two of his 29 field-goal attempts last season, he missed two field goals in nine attempts and one of six extra points in the first five games in 2026. In Miami's 31-24 home loss to the Cincinnati Bengals in Week 5, Patterson missed an extra-point try with 45 seconds remaining. For his career, Patterson has made 86.6% of his field-goal attempts (97 of 112) with a long of 54 in 66 games for six teams since 2021. McGraw, 24, has appeared in two games and has five tackles. An undrafted free agent out of Western Michigan, he signed to the Dolphins' practice squad on Sept. 10. Duck, 25, was placed on the reserve/physically unable to perform list on Aug. 30. He played in 16 games (four starts) for the Dolphins from 2024-25 and made 34 tackles and five passes defensed. Jones, who turns 28 on Sunday, played in three games for the Dolphins this season without recording a tackle. He played on 66% of the special teams snaps (45). Jones has career totals of 10 tackles and three passes defensed in 22 regular-season games (two starts) for the Washington Commanders (2023-24), Buffalo Bills (2025) and Dolphins. Washington selected him in the seventh round of the 2023 NFL Draft. Tucker, 36, starred for the Baltimore Ravens for 13 seasons, compiling the second-highest field-goal success rate (89.1%) in NFL history. The Super Bowl XLVII champion has not played since the league suspended him for 10 games in 2025 following allegations that Tucker engaged in inappropriate behavior during massage sessions. Tucker has denied the allegations. --Field Level Media

item.title: Rendimientos bonos Tesoro EEUU se alejan de sus mínimos gracias al repunte de la bolsa
item.description: Los rendimientos de los bonos del Tesoro estadounidense a más largo plazo bajaron el martes aunque se mantuvieron bastante por encima de los mínimos previos en una jornada volátil, mientras la bolsa estadounidense repuntaba en parte debido a un cambio de tendencia en las acciones del sector de la IA.
item.dc:creator: Chuck Mikolajczak
item.content:encoded: Los rendimientos de los bonos del Tesoro estadounidense a más largo plazo bajaron el martes aunque se mantuvieron bastante por encima de los mínimos previos en una jornada volátil, mientras la bolsa estadounidense repuntaba en parte debido a un cambio de tendencia en las acciones del sector de la IA. Los rendimientos bajaron la semana pasada, ya que la caída de las acciones de las empresas de infraestructura de IA, por la preocupación de que las inversiones pudieran agotarse a causa del aumento de los costos de financiación, desencadenó una demanda de bonos del Tesoro para refugio. A medida que se recuperaban de las pérdidas acciones como las de CoreWeave (CRWV.O) y el mercado bursátil en general repuntaba, los rendimientos se alejaron de sus mínimos previos, con los retornos a más corto plazo al alza durante la jornada. "El mercado está en medio de numerosas corrientes contrarias, y el panorama más amplio que ha impulsado al alza las tasas es el crecimiento, la alta inflación y la idea de que la Fed y los demás bancos centrales van a tomar medidas, lo que ha empujado al alza los retornos", dijo Robert Tipp, estratega jefe de inversiones y director de bonos globales de PGIM. "La cuestión es que las tasas a corto plazo y toda la curva de rendimientos se han adelantado a los bancos centrales, lo que ha provocado que se descuente un endurecimiento monetario enorme en un entorno en el que es poco probable que los bancos centrales suban las tasas rápidamente", destacó. "Esto ha dejado al mercado vulnerable a un retroceso brusco, una caída repentina de los rendimientos, y el detonante de ello ha sido la inquietud en torno al sector tecnológico", añadió. El rendimiento del bono del Tesoro a 10 años cayó 1,5 puntos básicos al 5,121% tras registrar un mínimo del 5,073% durante la sesión. Las expectativas de que la Reserva Federal suba las tasas al menos 25 puntos básicos en su reunión de política monetaria de la próxima semana se sitúan en el 17,2%, según el CME FedWatch, por debajo del 22,1% de hace una semana y del 57,6% de hace un mes. El retorno a 30 años descendió 4,2 puntos básicos, al 5,431%. La rentabilidad a dos años , que suele evolucionar en consonancia con las expectativas sobre las tasas de interés de la Fed, ganó 3 puntos básicos al 4,791%, tras caer al 4,734% más temprano. Un indicador muy seguido de la curva de rendimientos del Tesoro, que mide la diferencia entre las tasas a dos y 10 años , se situó en 32,8 puntos básicos positivos.

item.title: Carrefour warns of up to €200 million hit from riots and looting
item.description: Carrefour cut its annual earnings forecast on Tuesday, blaming an "unprecedented situation" in France as riots, looting and curfews raised costs and disrupted trading at its stores.
item.dc:creator: Helen Reid, Dominique Vidalon
item.content:encoded: Carrefour (CARR.PA) cut its annual earnings forecast on Tuesday, blaming an "unprecedented situation" in France as [USN:L6N4660DJ TEXT:"riots, looting and curfews"] raised costs and disrupted trading at its stores. The supermarket chain said it now expects "stable to slight" growth in 2026 adjusted earnings per share, having previously forecast growth in a high single-digit percentage. It also forecast a slight decline in free cash flow compared with 2025. Adding to widespread criticism of the government's policing efforts, Carrefour CEO Alexandre Bompard said he hoped security would be better for the next protests planned on October 24, but that he expects a business impact regardless. "Carrefour was directly and strongly affected. Around 50 of our stores were hit on day one, many were looted and the damage is considerable," Bompard said on a call with analysts. "Many of our teams and partners faced deeply distressing situations," he added, saying the retailer is helping workers to reopen affected stores as soon as it is safe. The unrest is hurting consumer confidence that was already weak because of high fuel prices and is reducing footfall at Carrefour stores as the key fourth-quarter trading period begins. Finance chief Matthieu Malige said the total impact could be between €80 million ($90 million) and €200 million of operating income. "The direct costs add up to several tens of millions of euros ... of stolen or destroyed merchandise, damaged stores, damaged equipment, and then there are also the stores we were forced to close," Malige told reporters. "In the weeks to come we will continue to be impacted as some stores have to close earlier due to curfews, and more broadly we think we're in a new situation marked by deep uncertainty for our customers." Many of Carrefour's 6,000 stores across the country were closed in anticipation of unrest, including on Sunday and Monday, Malige said, declining to disclose the total number of stores shut. Costs have increased as stores took measures to protect themselves, including the hiring of external security guards, Malige said, adding that Carrefour was among the most affected retailers because of its wide network of convenience stores in cities such as Paris, Lyon, and Marseille. As a result, Carrefour said it would invest less in France, cutting its capital expenditure forecast for the year to €1.6 billion from €1.7 billion. The retailer had been gearing up to begin its Black Friday sales events in the coming days, Malige added. ($1 = 0.8906 euros)

item.title: Albania formalises corruption charges against ex-deputy PM Balluku
item.description: Prosecutors in Albania have formalised corruption charges against former deputy prime minister Belinda Balluku, whose original indictment a year ago triggered rioting in Tirana.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Prosecutors in Albania have formalised corruption charges against former deputy prime minister Belinda Balluku, whose original indictment a year ago triggered rioting in Tirana. Balluku, who served as deputy to Prime Minister Edi Rama and also as an infrastructure minister, was charged [USN:L6N3WW0RW TEXT:"late last year"] with interfering in the award of two construction contracts in 2021 worth more than €200 million ($225 million). Corruption in public institutions has been one of the drivers this month of new, student-led protests and rioting in the capital Tirana calling for Rama to step down. On Tuesday, protesters gathered outside an education ministry building shouting "Balluku to jail!", and were pushed back by police using water cannon and tear gas. Balluku, 53, has made no public comment since denying wrongdoing in response to the original charges. Rama dismissed her in February but an attempt to strip her of her parliamentary immunity, which prevents her being arrested, failed. She did not respond to a request for comment on Tuesday. In an emailed statement to media, the Special Prosecution Office, which handles high-level corruption, said the final charges against Balluku included violation of the equality of participants in public tenders or auctions, and passive corruption of persons including high-ranking state officials. She was also charged with laundering the proceeds of criminal activity. "The Special Prosecution Office is continuing to take concrete procedural steps to formally communicate the charges to the other individuals involved in the same criminal case," it said. Rama, who has refused to step down, has condemned the violence. He said that the government would consider lowering the age for criminal liability and imposing a social media ban for those under 16 years old to counter the protests. ($1 = 0.8888 euros)

item.title: US senior housing operator Discovery Senior Living explores sale, sources say
item.description: The owners of Discovery Senior Living are exploring a sale of one of the largest senior housing operators in the US that could value it at more than $1 billion, according to two people familiar with the matter.
item.dc:creator: Abigail Summerville
item.content:encoded: The owners of Discovery Senior Living are exploring a sale of one of the largest senior housing operators in the US that could value it at more than $1 billion, according to two people familiar with the matter. The company, which operates and manages around 450 senior living and retirement communities in 40 states, is working with investment bank William Blair on the process, the people said, speaking on the condition of anonymity because the matter is private. Private equity firms Lee Equity Partners and Coastwood Senior Housing Partners invested in Discovery in 2022. The company generates around $65 million of annual earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization, the people said. Discovery, William Blair, and Lee Equity did not respond to requests for comment. Coastwood could not be reached for comment. Investors have been drawn to the residential property management sector for its recurring fees and exposure to housing demand without having to own the underlying real estate. For example, New Mountain Capital agreed to buy Asset Living, which provides services to multifamily, student, and affordable housing communities, for over $2 billion, Reuters [USN:L6N42616X TEXT:"reported "]in June. The senior housing sector, in particular, is drawing investor interest as baby boomers reach retirement age. On its website, Discovery describes senior housing as a "ground-floor opportunity to capitalize on a once-in-a-generation megatrend for investors and our society." Discovery uses a regional management model in which it partners with real estate investment trusts and other investors who own the underlying real estate. The Bonita Springs, Florida-based company agreed to buy Oregon-based Sunshine Retirement Living earlier this month, expanding in the Pacific Northwest. The underlying Sunshine communities will remain under existing ownership, including Sabra Healthcare REIT and Investcorp, the deal announcement said. Discovery, founded in the 1990s, operates communities including Discovery Village and Aston Gardens in Florida, Conservatory in Texas, and Rittenhouse Village in Pennsylvania and other states.

item.title: Bayern's Kompany, Kimmich, Neuer doubtful for Arsenal clash, says assistant coach
item.description: Bayern Munich could be without coach Vincent Kompany, first-choice goalkeeper Manuel Neuer and playmaker Joshua Kimmich when they host Arsenal in the Champions League on Wednesday, assistant coach Aaron Danks said on Tuesday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Bayern Munich could be without coach Vincent Kompany, first-choice goalkeeper Manuel Neuer and playmaker Joshua Kimmich when they host Arsenal in the Champions League on Wednesday, assistant coach Aaron Danks said on Tuesday. Kompany is nursing a virus that has affected his legs at times, while Neuer has only just recovered from a minor injury and Kimmich missed training due to personal reasons, Danks told a press conference. "Vince has had a virus, and it is important for him to rest," Danks said. "So he is at home. We are taking it day by day. He will play his role in the game whether in the Allianz Arena or not." As for Neuer, no decision has yet been made, Danks said, with the keeper back in training for the past two days. Kimmich's participation is equally unclear. "For Joshua it is personal reasons. I am not sure what it means for tomorrow," Danks added. Bayern, already without suspended Michael Olise, want to bounce back in the competition after last week's 3-3 [USN:L6N45Z15P TEXT:"draw"] against Viking in Norway, and have been boosted by a 6-1 [USN:L6N46305Y TEXT:"demolition"] of RB Leipzig in the Bundesliga on Saturday. "The key will be decided on small margins," Danks said. "We have to be prepared for every aspect of the game. "We trust the process and the work we have done with the players in the last couple of seasons. We want them to play fearless and express themselves."

item.title: US coaxing refiners to produce more diesel, energy department officials say
item.description: Two top US energy department officials said on Tuesday they were working with refiners at home and abroad to boost fuel output as a diesel shortage raises worries about prices and inflation ahead of the November midterm elections.
item.dc:creator: Nathan Crooks, Arathy Somasekhar
item.content:encoded: Two top US energy department officials said on Tuesday they were working with refiners at home and abroad to boost fuel output as a diesel shortage raises worries about prices and inflation ahead of the November [TOPIC:"reuters:/world/us/elections/" TEXT:"midterm elections"]. The Trump administration has taken several steps to try to lower fuel prices that have surged since the start of the Iran war on February 28, including relaxing restrictions on Russian diesel exports, invoking the Defense Production Act to boost output, and allowing commercial vehicles to run on red-dyed diesel normally limited to off-road equipment. Diesel is critical to the global economy, powering much of the transport, agriculture and heavy industry that underpin global trade and economic activity. "We are talking about reopening every refinery we can," Energy Secretary Chris Wright said in Houston. "There are dialogues there, and that's a tough challenge. I'm not saying all these are going to happen." Diesel prices have jumped to record highs as the Iran war continues and as Ukraine attacks Russian refineries. Retail diesel prices averaged about $6.32 a gallon on Tuesday, according to motorist group AAA. DIFFICULT TO RAISE US OUTPUT US refineries are running near full capacity, and with several facilities shutting in recent years, there is little leeway to quickly boost domestic output, analysts say. [USN:L6N3Q20MK TEXT:"Refinery expansions"] are capital intensive and take months, if not years, to complete depending on the complexity of the additions. Wright said the US is also working with India to increase refining output there to bring products to global markets. American Petroleum Institute CEO Mike Sommers told Reuters on the sidelines of an energy forum in Titusville, Pennsylvania that US refiners are running at 95% to 100% of capacity. He said they are putting off planned maintenance because of high prices. “The American refiners are doing everything they can,” Sommers said. He said that using the Defense Production Act to restart idled plants, as the administration has floated, would require a lot of capital. Last week, Vice President JD Vance said the administration would use the DPA to [USN:L6N45Z1BU TEXT:"expand capacity"] of a Texas refinery owned by Delek US Holdings (DK.N) . President Donald Trump signed legislation last year that included $1 billion in DPA funding for energy-related projects deemed critical to national security. Wright said there was "more to do" on refining and the DPA but did not provide additional details. Sommers singled out spare refining capacity in China, which he described as currently barring diesel exports. Beijing “is really going to be the key if we’re going to get long-term prices down,” he said. The Chinese embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment. PUSH FOR EUROPEAN DIESEL Trump [USN:S0N43U024 TEXT:"temporarily waived sanctions"] this month on Russian diesel in an attempt to lower prices. Russian diesel will likely move to New England, if it moves to the US at all, Wright said. Already, cargoes from Russia are returning to their[USN:L6N4660PS TEXT:" traditional destinations"] after the US suspended sanctions, with two tankers signaling trips to Turkey and Brazil in recent days, Reuters reported on Tuesday. The Trump administration has also been pushing Europe to release more fuel to balance global markets. "We are working with our friends ... to find new and innovative ways to get more throughput" through refineries, said Energy Department Undersecretary Kyle Haustveit at the Drake Forum in Titusville. While the Trump administration has pushed Europe to release 50 million barrels of diesel, an agreement by industrialized nations fell short. The Paris-based International Energy Agency said last week it would speed the release of crude and oil product volumes pledged in March, including more than 20 million barrels of diesel as soon as possible. Fatih Birol, chief of the IEA, which coordinates industrialized nations' releases of oil from emergency stocks, said on Tuesday the [USN:L6N4660MV TEXT:"group is ready"] to coordinate more oil releases by member countries if needed.

item.title: Starboard's Smith unveils stake in Solstice, presses for improvements
item.description: Activist investor Starboard Value on Tuesday unveiled a new stake in Honeywell spin-off Solstice Advanced Materials , arguing the company is undervalued and needs someone to hold management accountable for boosting share price performance.
item.dc:creator: Svea Herbst-Bayliss
item.content:encoded: Activist investor Starboard Value on Tuesday unveiled a new stake in Honeywell spin-off Solstice Advanced Materials (SOLS.O) , arguing the company is undervalued and needs someone to hold management accountable for boosting share price performance. Solstice is trading "stupid cheap," Starboard managing member and chief executive Jeffrey Smith said at the annual 13D Monitor Active-Passive Investor Summit in New York. Solstice has "great businesses but is undervalued," Smith said, attributing the discount to the market losing faith in management's ability to get the best out of its core business lines. To improve performance, management should focus on its core refrigerants and nuclear businesses and cut roughly $100 million in costs across the company, Smith said. “Solstice regularly engages with its shareowners and welcomes feedback aimed at enhancing shareowner value. We will review Starboard’s presentation carefully and look forward to engaging with the firm," a company representative said in a statement. "Our Board of Directors and management team remain committed to acting in the best interests of all Solstice shareowners." Spun out of Honeywell (HON.O) a year ago, Solstice initially saw its share price gain significantly. However, it is down roughly 30% since closing at an all-time high on June 30, in part having failed to recover from an aborted $14.5 billion deal to buy specialty chemicals company Element Solutions (ESI.N) . The [USN:L4N4380RV TEXT:"cash-and-stock deal"] was announced on July 6, and was billed as a way for Solstice to capitalize on growing demand from data centers and the chip industries. However, following feedback from shareholders on both sides, the companies [USN:L4N44O21D TEXT:"canceled the agreement"] on August 27. Smith also discussed the firm's investment in Knife River Corp (KNF.N) , where Reuters [USN:L1N4650SX TEXT:"reported"] on Monday that Starboard has lined up director candidates for election to the company's board. On Tuesday, Smith said that the company is "a very attractive acquisition target." Since making its investment public in September, Starboard has pushed Knife River to boost its profit margins. The company did not respond to a request for comment from Reuters.

item.title: 0ver 120 international players on NBA opening-night rosters
item.description: Opening-night rosters will feature 125 international players, the NBA said on Tuesday, with France becoming the first country outside Canada in 13 seasons to lead the league in international representatives.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Opening-night rosters will feature 125 international players, the NBA said on Tuesday, with France becoming the first country outside Canada in 13 seasons to lead the league in international representatives. The 2026-27 season tips off on Tuesday, marking the 13th consecutive year where at least 100 international players are on opening-night rosters, with 43 countries represented across six continents. France is the most-represented outside the US with 17 players, a group headlined by San Antonio Spurs' twice All-Star and reigning Defensive Player of the Year Victor Wembanyama. Canada, which for the past 12 seasons had led the league in international players, is next with 16 players, followed by Australia (9), Germany (7), Nigeria (6) and Serbia (6). The Dallas Mavericks, Miami Heat and Washington Wizards feature a league-high seven international players each. The NBA said there were 70 European players on opening-night rosters, including the Heat's Giannis Antetokounmpo (Greece), Denver Nuggets' Nikola Jokic (Serbia) and Los Angeles Lakers' Luka Doncic (Slovenia). The league is staging three games outside of the US and Canada this season as part of its efforts to grow the game globally. Denver and Indiana will meet in Mexico City on November 7 before January games between New Orleans and San Antonio in Paris and Manchester.

item.title: US health agency confirms third measles-related death this year
item.description: The United States has logged a third measles-related death this year, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said on Tuesday, as the country battles its worst outbreak in decades.
item.dc:creator: Kamal Choudhury
item.content:encoded: The United States has logged a third measles-related death this year, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said on Tuesday, as the country battles its worst outbreak in decades. The toll matches the previous year's total, with the agency reporting 4,410 confirmed cases nationwide as of October 15. CDC had reported [USN:L4N45L13A TEXT:"two deaths"] related to the once-eliminated disease in September. The US Department of Health and Human Services, which oversees the CDC, told Reuters that the National Center for Health Statistics received a report of a measles-related death and verified that the disease was the underlying cause. The CDC did not name the states where the deaths occurred. STATE TALLIES AND FEDERAL AID The federal death toll remains lower than figures reported by local health authorities, with Pennsylvania recording [USN:L4N45M1NB TEXT:"five confirmed"] measles-associated deaths — all in unvaccinated individuals — as of October 19. The gap in numbers follows a policy shift under US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., with the CDC switching to NCHS mortality data to track measles deaths, replacing its earlier reliance on state health departments' figures. "We should not have any measles deaths in the United States," said William Moss, an epidemiology professor at Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, noting the disease was declared eliminated in the country in 2000. He called for stronger federal efforts to boost [USN:L6N45614T TEXT:"vaccination"] in vulnerable communities and tackle misinformation. Last week, the CDC agreed to deploy [USN:L4N45Z1Q3 TEXT:"additional support to Pennsylvania"] to help investigate the outbreak. The state, which has been hit hardest by the resurgence, has logged 1,286 cases, and officials are reviewing an [USN:L4N45Y148 TEXT:"additional death"] reported by the Franklin County coroner. In neighboring New York, the state health department reported 162 measles cases as of October 17. Governor Kathy Hochul declared a statewide [USN:L4N45R1BM TEXT:"disaster emergency"] earlier this month and said she would seek [USN:L4N45U0P8 TEXT:"federal help"]. Measles is a highly contagious viral disease but can be prevented through the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine, which is about 97% effective after two doses.

item.title: Eastern Libya parliament approves maritime deal with Turkey, drawing Greek rejection
item.description: Libya's eastern parliament approved a maritime boundaries deal with Turkey on Tuesday, drawing swift condemnation from Greece which called it a violation of international law.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Libya's eastern parliament approved a maritime boundaries deal with Turkey on Tuesday, drawing swift condemnation from Greece which called it a violation of international law. The deal is part of a years-old dispute over competing claims to sea borders and energy exploration rights in the eastern Mediterranean. It was [USN:KBN1Y21VL TEXT:"originally agreed"] in 2019 by Libya’s internationally recognised government in Tripoli in the west, but the rival eastern administration under military commander Khalifa Haftar had withheld its approval for years. Greece, Egypt and Cyprus have long been [USN:KBN1Y82JB TEXT:"opposed to the deal,"] which they see as infringing on their own maritime claims. In a foreign ministry statement, Athens said the deal "remains illegal, null and void, contravenes international law of the sea, and infringes upon the sovereign rights of states in the region." "We call on the Libyan side to refrain from any action that contravenes International Law and undermines stability in the Eastern Mediterranean," it said. Turkey's foreign ministry welcomed the Libyan parliament's decision, saying the agreement respected the mutual rights and interests of both countries under international law and the principles of equity. "Turkey will continue its determination to work together with all partners to ensure security, stability and peace in the Mediterranean basin," the ministry said. Athens and Cairo signed an overlapping deal designating an exclusive economic zone in the eastern Mediterranean in 2020, which Turkey opposes. Last year, Greece approved hydrocarbon exploration for a consortium led by US major Chevron south of Crete, [USN:L6N3ZF0GI TEXT:"condemned by Ankara"] as "unlawful." WARMING RELATIONS Libya broke apart into rival eastern and western administrations more than a decade ago during a civil war after longtime Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi was toppled by a NATO-backed uprising. Turkish support was crucial to repelling an assault by Haftar's forces on Tripoli in 2019-2020. But relations have steadily improved in recent years, with Turkish officials paying regular visits to Haftar’s de facto capital, Benghazi, and investing heavily in construction and other sectors. In the same session, the eastern parliament also reversed a 2020 decision to cut off political ties with Ankara. The move to ratify the deal marks a "complete reversal" which "reveals the depth of the relationship between Ankara and Benghazi today," said Anas El Gomati, head of the Sadeq Institute, a Libyan think tank. The vote had been eased by the replacement earlier this month of the long-serving parliament speaker, Aguila Saleh, widely seen as an ally of Egypt, he added. Saddam Haftar, the deputy of Haftar, welcomed parliament's approval in a statement, calling the deal "a tool that can help protect Libya’s rights and economic interests in the Mediterranean." Libyan lawmaker Tarek al-Jeroushi told Reuters the agreement would strengthen Libya's position as a political, military and economic partner to major powers. "Some countries may be upset by this agreement, but what matters to us is our national interest," he said. Jalel Harchaoui, a contributor to Britain's Royal United Services Institute think tank, said the vote could also open the way to an expanded Turkish military presence in the east. "Today's parliamentary ratification is a watershed," he said.

item.title: El dólar cae mientras los operadores evalúan los riesgos por Irán y la inteligencia artificial
item.description: El dólar estadounidense se depreció el martes, en línea con una caída de los precios del petróleo y de los rendimientos de los bonos del Tesoro de más largo plazo, mientras los operadores evaluaban el impacto del aumento de la tensión en la guerra de Estados Unidos con Irán y la sostenibilidad de las fuertes entradas de capital hacia las empresas estadounidenses de IA.
item.dc:creator: Karen Brettell
item.content:encoded: El dólar estadounidense se depreció el martes, en línea con una caída de los precios del petróleo y de los rendimientos de los bonos del Tesoro de más largo plazo, mientras los operadores evaluaban el impacto del aumento de la tensión en la guerra de Estados Unidos con Irán y la sostenibilidad de las fuertes entradas de capital hacia las empresas estadounidenses de IA. Los precios del petróleo bajaron, tras alcanzar su máximo en cinco meses, mientras los operadores seguían una reunión entre el presidente iraní y el jefe del ejército pakistaní —un mediador clave— y los continuos ataques hutíes contra infraestructuras sauditas,además de las noticias sobre ataques a buques en el Golfo. El aumento de los precios del petróleo ha suscitado el temor a que la inflación se mantenga alta durante más tiempo. El dólar se disparó la semana pasada después de que datos mostraron que la inflación de los precios al consumo en Estados Unidos se aceleró en septiembre. Pero el movimiento pronto quedó eclipsado por las preocupaciones sobre la IA. "El aumento de los precios de la energía es positivo para el dólar, pero si se llega a un punto en el que las tasas suben tanto que el comercio relacionado con la IA se desploma, de repente tiene un impacto negativo", dijo Dominic Bunning, responsable de estrategia de divisas del G-10 en Nomura. "Hay un umbral ahí y, en estos momentos, estamos rozándolo". Las fuertes entradas de capital en la bolsa estadounidense han respaldado al dólar. El aumento de las tasas de interés, impulsado en parte por las expectativas de crecimiento e inflación vinculadas al sector, también ha contribuido a ello. * El índice dólar , que mide la cotización de la moneda estadounidense frente a una cesta de seis divisas que incluye al yen y al euro, cayó un 0,25% a 101,71, mientras que el euro subió un 0,22% a 1,1235 dólares. * Los operadores se mantenían cautelosos con respecto al euro a pesar de las modestas subidas del martes, ya que Francia se enfrenta a protestas generalizadas y a un panorama fiscal cada vez más sombrío. * El Gobierno dijo que los toques de queda nocturnos en las zonas afectadas por la violencia de las principales ciudades francesas habían supuesto un respiro frente a los peores disturbios que ha vivido el país en años. Se prevén más protestas para el fin de semana. * La libra esterlina se apreció un 0,59%, a 1,338 dólares, después de que los datos del mercado laboral mostraron un mercado laboral resistente, la última serie de datos del Reino Unido que sorprendió al alza. * Según datos de LSEG, los mercados están descontando casi por completo una subida de tasas de 25 puntos básicos por parte del Banco de Inglaterra en su próxima reunión, el 5 de noviembre. * El yen subía después de que una subasta de bonos del Estado japonés (JGB) a largo plazo registró una demanda récord. La moneda japonesa ganó un 0,21% frente al dólar, a 158,14 unidades por dólar.

item.title: Salesforce deepens AI bets with $5.66 billion Braze deal
item.description: Salesforce is buying Braze in a deal valued at about $5.66 billion, bolstering its AI push with tools that let brands send personalized messages and respond to customer behavior in real time.
item.dc:creator: Anzar Mehraj
item.content:encoded: Salesforce (CRM.N) is buying Braze (BRZE.O) in a deal valued at about $5.66 billion, bolstering its AI push with tools that let brands send personalized messages and respond to customer behavior in real time. Shares of Braze jumped more than 50% on Tuesday after the deal was announced. The deal is the latest bet by Salesforce to accelerate its AI transition as investors worry that the rapid adoption of the technology could erode demand for traditional software. Braze shareholders will receive $47.50 in cash per share held, representing a premium of about 58.1% to the stock's last close. Braze serves about 2,770 customers, including Canva, Instacart and Venmo, with AI tools that help marketers optimize content, offers and channels. Salesforce is essentially buying "a real-time engagement layer that its marketing business has historically lacked," said Shay Boloor, chief market strategist at Futurum Equities. The company, which provides customer relationship management software, expects the transaction to close in its fiscal 2028 and does not see deal changing its fiscal 2027 forecast. Salesforce has been doubling down on its AI offering and signed a $3.6 billion deal for [USN:L6N42N0XU TEXT:"AI agent platform Fin"] earlier this year and an $8 billion deal for [USN:L3N3RZ0OR TEXT:"Informatica"] last year. The San Francisco-based company would pay a $300 million termination fee, while Braze would pay $191.4 million if it abandons the deal. J.P. Morgan Securities is the exclusive financial adviser to Salesforce, while Qatalyst Partners is advising Braze.

item.title: Kroger to invest $5 billion by 2029 as new CEO sharpens grocery focus
item.description: Kroger unveiled a $5 billion investment plan to lower prices and improve the shopping experience, as part of new CEO Greg Foran's first strategy to revive the grocer's core business amid intensifying competition and cautious consumer spending.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Kroger (KR.N) unveiled a $5 billion investment plan to lower prices and improve the shopping experience, as part of new CEO Greg Foran's first strategy to revive the grocer's core business amid intensifying competition and cautious consumer spending. The company on Tuesday also set a target of about 3% core comparable sales growth by 2029, sending shares up as much as 2.6%. Here are some details: The investment, which will be realized by 2029, would also focus on simplifying promotions, elevating merchandising, refreshing store formats and boosting loyalty programs, the company said during its investor day "A $5 billion investment in customer value is the largest single driver in this plan and it is entirely self-funded," CFO David Kennerley said Ahead of the investor day, Kroger said it would invest in fresh foods, prepared meals, private-label products and its membership program Foran, who [USN:L4N3Z50WX TEXT:"became"] CEO in February, said in a memo this month that Kroger plans to cut about a third of its corporate roles over three years, using AI to reduce duplicative work Kroger also said on Tuesday it would target growth in e-commerce and retail media for higher-margin revenue options

item.title: Italy's Meloni approves tougher anti-riot laws after Milan violence
item.description: Italy approved a raft of security measures on Tuesday including a new offence of violent participation in a demonstration, tougher penalties for rioters, and financial liability for parents whose children take part in vandalism and looting.
item.dc:creator: Giuseppe Fonte, Emilio Parodi, Anna Uras
item.content:encoded: Italy approved a raft of security measures on Tuesday including a new offence of violent participation in a demonstration, tougher penalties for rioters, and financial liability for parents whose children take part in vandalism and looting. The move came after unrest swept northern Italian cities at the weekend, including the financial capital Milan, where gangs of mainly young people went on the rampage, smashing windows, robbing shops and attacking police. "There is nothing revolutionary about vandalising and stealing. Vandalism and theft are not protest, they are criminality," Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said on social media, unveiling the decree. As part of the package, which comes into immediate effect, anyone who takes part in a group of at least five people and endangers public safety during protests faces up to five years in prison and a maximum fine of €20,000 ($22,460). Penalties increase if faces are concealed or people injured. Authorities are empowered to order prompt compensation for any damage inflicted and, in the case of minors, their parents will be held liable. Police will be allowed to detain youths aged between 14 and 17, even if they have not committed a crime, provided there is evidence they pose a danger, extending powers that previously applied only to adults. While authorities fear further unrest at demonstrations planned for Saturday, the government said it would deploy [USN:L1N4650LE TEXT:"500 army troops"] alongside the police in Milan until the end of 2026. The military will help reinforce security at key sites, step up surveillance of sensitive locations and enhance monitoring across the area, the defence ministry said in a statement. MELONI'S SECURITY CRACKDOWN The disturbances in northern Italy echoed riots in [USN:L1N46401W TEXT:"neighbouring France"], where hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets on Saturday in some of the country's most violent turmoil in years. Meloni has passed [USN:L8N4661UE TEXT:"a steady stream"] of security crackdowns since taking office in 2022, which critics say do little to address the underlying causes of crime and disorder. Italy's prison population has increased by more than 17% over four years, or nearly 10,000 people, government data shows. Meloni's government is also facing mounting pressure from a separate wave of [USN:L1N4660JW TEXT:"protests in southern Italy"], where truck drivers angered by soaring diesel prices and the rising cost of living have staged roadblocks that are disrupting supply chains. Some pasta makers have had to halt production and agricultural groups have warned that fruit and vegetables could be left to rot. The government has promised fresh aid for road hauliers after talks with industry representatives. Protesters in both the north and the south say rising prices are pushing families into poverty -- a concern for Meloni ahead of national elections that are due in 2027. "We know what it means to look for a job, to earn an insufficient wage, and to see no prospects for the future ... but hardship must never be used as an excuse for violence," the prime minister said on Tuesday. ($1 = 0.8906 euros)

item.title: Turkey submits Saudi-Pakistan defence pact to parliament for ratification, sources say
item.description: Turkey has submitted a defence pact with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia to parliament for ratification, three parliamentary sources said on Tuesday, moving NATO's second-largest army closer to a formal mutual defence pledge with Riyadh as it faces Houthi attacks.
item.dc:creator: Huseyin Hayatsever, Nevzat Devranoglu, Ece Toksabay
item.content:encoded: Turkey has submitted a defence pact with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia to parliament for ratification, three parliamentary sources said on Tuesday, moving NATO's second-largest army closer to a formal mutual defence pledge with Riyadh as it faces Houthi attacks. The three countries signed [USN:L6N4440IT TEXT:"the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement"] in August, under which an armed attack on one member is considered an attack on all. The agreement's first article says the parties shall use "all necessary means" to eliminate threats to one another's territorial integrity, sovereignty or internationally recognised borders, according to a text seen by Reuters. "In the event one of the parties is subjected to an armed attack or military aggression by another country or group of countries, the parties shall immediately provide assistance to the party under attack, utilising the full range of mutual assistance measures available to them," Article 2 of the agreement says. The provision, similar to NATO's Article 5, refers to Article 51 of the UN Charter, which covers the individual or collective right of states to self-defence against armed attack. The three countries "will decide on the scope and nature of the support to be provided following an objective assessment of the assistance required" and will cooperate within their available resources, including military capabilities and resources, the same article says. At an emergency meeting of the alliance in Riyadh earlier this month, the three countries agreed to ensure the "rapid deployment" of military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia. Turkey, which has a robust defence industry, has condemned Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, expressed willingness to help meet Riyadh's military technology needs and agreed to join a Saudi-led coalition to ensure navigational safety in the Red Sea. The agreement also envisages close cooperation on defence industry, intelligence sharing, logistical support and the fight against "all means of terrorism," including at the operational level. Parliamentary ratification is required for Turkey to formally approve the agreement. AIM TO "STRENGTHEN COLLECTIVE DETERRENCE" Parliament Speaker Numan Kurtulmus, currently visiting Kyrgyzstan, will refer the agreement to parliament's foreign affairs commission upon his return, two of the sources said. The contents and details of the agreement are expected to become public once it is submitted to the commission. The commission could debate the agreement as early as Friday, another source said. President Tayyip Erdogan's communications director, Burhanettin Duran, said that Turkey's recent step marked an important milestone towards the institutionalisation of strategic cooperation between the three nations. "This strategic partnership developed between our countries aims to strengthen collective deterrence, enhance joint capabilities in the defence sector, and safeguard security and stability in our region," Duran said in a post on X. A Turkish official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said Turkey's own contribution was expected to be limited to [USN:L6N45T0WB TEXT:" military equipment"], intelligence sharing and weapons systems, adding that no other form of deployment had taken place under the alliance so far. Asked how Turkey could help Saudi Arabia defend against attacks by Yemen's Houthis, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said that the Mecca Agreement was not an "offensive agreement," adding that Turkey [USN:L6N45U0RL TEXT:"would not send troops"] to another country to carry out attacks on its territory. Turkey's constitution requires separate permission from parliament to deploy troops abroad regardless of any international agreement.

item.title: Israeli fire kills four people in Gaza, medics say
item.description: Israeli strikes and gunfire killed at least four Palestinians, including a married couple and a 17-year-old, in separate incidents in the Gaza Strip on Tuesday, health officials said.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Israeli strikes and gunfire killed at least four Palestinians, including a married couple and a 17-year-old, in separate incidents in the Gaza Strip on Tuesday, health officials said. Medics said an Israeli airstrike killed Akram Yassin and his wife Dina Abu Baker in an apartment in Gaza City. The Israeli military said in a statement hours later that Yassin was a senior official in Hamas's general security apparatus in the Gaza Strip. It said the apparatus was tasked with protecting senior Hamas officials. In Khan Younis, in the south, medics said a 17-year-old boy was killed by Israeli gunfire near the Qizan Al-Najar neighbourhood, while another was killed by Israeli gunfire in the Zeitoun suburb east of Gaza City, taking Tuesday's death toll to at least four. The Israeli military did not immediately comment on either of the two gunfire incidents. Palestinians inspected the aftermath of the strike on the apartment in Gaza City before gathering for the couple's funeral. "We’re supposed to be in a ceasefire period, but honestly, we are not seeing a ceasefire or anything. The war is still going on, assassinations are continuing, and the shelling has not stopped," said Mahmoud Yassin, whose brother was killed. Israel, which says the Hamas militant group has been rearming and launching attacks in violation of the ceasefire, has stepped up strikes on the group in recent weeks. Hamas has denied trying to carry out attacks or rebuild its arsenal and accuses Israel of undermining the Gaza peace deal. The ceasefire, brokered by the US a year ago, calls for the eventual reconstruction of the territory. But little progress has been made towards implementing a deal to end the conflict that includes terms for Hamas to disarm and Israel to withdraw its troops. Gaza health officials have said at least 1,500 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli fire since the ceasefire. Israel says four of its soldiers have been killed by militants in Gaza over the same period.

item.title: El oro baja mientras los inversores analizan las señales de la Fed
item.description: El oro cerró con un ligero descenso el martes, mientras los inversionistas sopesaban la probabilidad de nuevas subidas de las tasas de interés en Estados Unidos este año, a la espera de la reunión sobre política monetaria de la Reserva Federal de la próxima semana.
item.dc:creator: Anushree Mukherjee
item.content:encoded: El oro cerró con un ligero descenso el martes, mientras los inversionistas sopesaban la probabilidad de nuevas subidas de las tasas de interés en Estados Unidos este año, a la espera de la reunión sobre política monetaria de la Reserva Federal de la próxima semana. El oro al contado bajó un 0,3%, a 4.125,90 dólares por onza, a las 1805 GMT, mientras que los futuros en Estados Unidos cerraron con un descenso del 0,4%, a 4.142,60 dólares por onza. "La inflación y las tasas de interés de la Fed son los grandes retos a los que se enfrenta el oro en estos momentos. Los bonos del Tesoro de Estados Unidos parecen, por el momento, una opción más favorable que el oro como activo refugio", dijo Bob Haberkorn, estratega senior de mercados de StoneX. "Los 4.000 dólares son un nivel importante al que hay que prestar atención para ver si el oro puede mantenerse por encima. En gran medida, eso dependerá, por el momento, de lo que diga la Fed", añadió Haberkorn. La Fed subió las tasas de interés un cuarto de punto en septiembre, la primera alza de este año. Si bien los recientes comentarios de los responsables de la Fed, que apuntan a que no hay mucha urgencia por un mayor endurecimiento de la política monetaria, han moderado las expectativas de una subida de tasas en la reunión de política monetaria del banco central del 27 al 28 de octubre, los operadores ven un 92% de probabilidad de que haya una en diciembre, según la herramienta FedWatch de CME. El oro sigue registrando una caída de alrededor del 26% desde su máximo histórico de 5.594,82 dólares de enero, y de aproximadamente un 22% desde el comienzo de la guerra en Irán, cuando las preocupaciones por la inflación impulsada por la energía reforzaron las apuestas por subidas de las tasas de interés. El índice de gastos de consumo personal (PCE) de Estados Unidos, el indicador de inflación preferido por el banco central y que se publicará la próxima semana, también está en el punto de mira de los inversores en busca de pistas sobre las perspectivas de las tasas de interés. Por otra parte, en Japón, el gobernador del banco central, Kazuo Ueda, dijo que la inflación subyacente estaba "bastante cerca" del objetivo del 2%, lo que apunta a un margen para nuevas subidas de tasas. Entre otros metales, la plata al contado subió un 1,4%, a 57,86 dólares por onza; el platino ganó un 1%, a 1.656,85 dólares por onza; y el paladio cayó un 1,3%, a 1.105,50 dólares por onza.

item.title: Wall Street rises with investors rotating into healthcare and value stocks
item.description: The Dow led Wall Street higher on Tuesday as investors focused on value stocks such as healthcare, while technology lagged after rebounding a day earlier.
item.dc:creator: Sinead Carew, Tharuniyaa Lakshmi
item.content:encoded: The Dow led Wall Street higher on Tuesday as investors focused on value stocks such as healthcare, while technology lagged after rebounding a day earlier. Healthcare (.SPXHC) led gains among the S&P 500's 11 major sector indexes and was up 2.3% after hitting a record high. Big gainers included drugmakers, such as Eli Lilly (LLY.N) , up almost 4% and the biggest boost to the benchmark index, and Moderna (MRNA.O) , up more than 5%. Real estate (.SPLRCR) and utility (.SPLRCU) sectors were also outperforming, with both up more than 1%, along with the small cap Russell 2000 index (.RUT) , which added 1.7%. Declines in megacap stocks pulled the communication services (.SPLRCL) sector down. Energy (.SPNY) shares were flat as[USN:L1N46601X TEXT:" oil prices"] dipped after touching a five-month high. Traders were weighing a meeting between the Iranian president and Pakistan's army chief, a key US-Iran mediator, against Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure and reports of vessel attacks in the Gulf. TECH STOCKS UP SLIGHTLY Technology stocks barely gained on Tuesday after rebounding sharply on Monday. Last week's selloff was fueled in part by concerns over the cost of financing for AI developments, with cloud company CoreWeave (CRWV.O) at the center of those worries. "Equity investors are still a little skeptical around the AI trade and the ability for some of these companies to monetize their investments, so you're seeing a bit of a rotation into other areas of the market," said Jim Baird, chief investment officer at Plante Moran Financial Advisors, pointing to advances in small caps and sectors including healthcare. "Investors are looking for other opportunities outside of tech, and healthcare is one of the beneficiaries of that," he said. At 2:08 p.m. ET (1808 GMT), the Dow Jones Industrial Average (.DJI) rose 518.51 points, or 1%, to 52,485.50, the S&P 500 (.SPX) gained 31.24 points, or 0.4%, to 7,721.44 and the Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) gained 54.84 points, or 0.2%, to 26,482.94. The Philadelphia Semiconductor (.SOX) index rose 0.5%. While the S&P 500 value index (.IVX) was up 0.8%, its growth counterpart (.IGX) was down 0.02%. Investors were looking ahead to earnings reports from SpaceX (SPCX.O) and Netflix (NFLX.O) , due after the market close. Meta and Tesla (TSLA.O) are scheduled to report on Wednesday. Meta (META.O) , down 2.2%, and Netflix, off 0.9%, were among the weakest stocks in communication services, along with Alphabet (GOOGL.O) , which lost more than 1%. General Motors (GM.N) shares dropped more than 8% and were the S&P 500's biggest laggards, after the automaker [USN:L6N4660PI TEXT:"signaled pressure in coming months"] from higher commodity costs and lower truck sales. 3M (MMM.N) gained 5.9% after the [USN:L4N4651MW TEXT:"company said"] it was expanding its data-center partnership with Amazon (AMZN.O) and issued a warrant to an Amazon subsidiary to purchase 3M common stock worth over $521 million. The industrial conglomerate also raised its full-year profit forecast. Credit reporting firm Equifax (EFX.N) jumped more than 10% after it reported third-quarter profit above analysts' estimates. It was among the S&P 500's biggest percentage gainers on the day, along with Hasbro (HAS.O) . The toymaker gained 10% after it [USN:L6N4660PC TEXT:"raised its full-year forecast"] for both overall revenue and its digital gaming business. Advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 2.46-to-1 ratio on the NYSE, where there were 97 new highs and 193 new lows. On the Nasdaq, 3,416 stocks rose and 1,269 fell as advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 2.69-to-1 ratio. The S&P 500 posted 22 new 52-week highs and one new low while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 39 new highs and 224 new lows.

item.title: Could disillusioned Kansas voters send their first Democrat to the US Senate in 94 years?
item.description: The last time the state of Kansas sent a Democrat to the US Senate, the Great Depression was ravaging the state, wheat prices had collapsed and drought was turning the Great Plains into the Dust Bowl.
item.dc:creator: Renee Hickman
item.content:encoded: The last time the state of Kansas sent a Democrat to the US Senate, the Great Depression was ravaging the state, wheat prices had collapsed and drought was turning the Great Plains into the Dust Bowl. Some 94 years later, Kansas may do it again. Democratic candidate Adam Hamilton, a megachurch pastor, is running neck and neck with Republican US Senator Roger Marshall, based on both a New York Times/Siena Poll and Emerson College Polling , in a state that Republican President Donald Trump won in 2024 with more than 57% of the vote. The unexpectedly competitive race reflects strains in the Republican heartland, where Democrats are betting that soaring farm costs, including near-record-high diesel, and discontent with Trump's immigration crackdown can revive the region's progressive populist tradition. In the converted grain bin that serves as an office for Vance and Louise Ehmke's wheat farm and seed business, John Brown, the abolitionist who took up arms against slavery in Kansas, stares down from a reproduction of a famous painting. In 1885, 20 years after the Civil War, Vance Ehmke’s ancestors started farming in western Kansas. But now, climbing costs linked to the US-Israeli war on Iran have him contemplating a dark future for his farm and others around it. “During the past year, we have seen fuel prices just darn near double,” Ehmke said. “That’s cost us $50,000 of unexpected expenses.” COST OF FUEL, FERTILIZER Fuel and fertilizer prices have [USN:L6N45S116 TEXT:"shot up"] dramatically since the war started in February, with [USN:L1N45U0FQ TEXT:"diesel"] used to power farm equipment up 70% since the war began. Those rising costs have reverberated in states like Kansas, Iowa and Nebraska, where agriculture dominates local economies. In Iowa, opinion polls show Republican US Representative Ashley Hinson in a tight Senate race with Democrat Josh Turek for the seat [USN:L6N45U0XV TEXT:"being vacated"] by Republican Joni Ernst. Hinson called last month for an "immediate end" to the Iran war in a social media post that said Iowans "shouldn't have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war." In Nebraska, Republican Senator Pete Ricketts faces a competitive race against independent Dan Osborn, despite Trump winning the state by more than 20 points in 2024. Democrats need to pick up four US Senate seats to win control of the chamber. TRUMP, JD VANCE STUMP FOR AT-RISK REPUBLICANS Trump, Vice President JD Vance and other leading Republicans have stumped for at-risk candidates in the Midwest region. Trump pledged in Nebraska this month to expand access to [USN:FWN45R168 TEXT:"tax-exempt diesel fuel"] and, in a Wichita-area rally on Monday, said the US Department of Agriculture would launch a "harvest fuel relief program" to provide farmers with [USN:SPN4650BH TEXT:"$8 billion"] to offset diesel costs during the harvest season. Hamilton still has an uphill climb with many rural Kansas voters. Not far from the Ehmkes is another farm owned by Ron Suppes, a Republican who supports Marshall. “We’ve had high diesel prices in prior years. I don’t know if it matters which administration,” he said. “I’ll put up with the pain for a while." Another Trump priority hit the Kansas meatpacking industry in late September, when Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents arrested 104 people in Dodge City, Garden City, Liberal and surrounding areas, according to the US Attorney's Office for the District of Kansas. Amid voter anger over high beef prices, the raids [USN:L1N45G16V TEXT:"slowed operations"] at major processors including Cargill and National Beef as some employees stayed home for fear of arrest. The raids may also have affected the traditionally conservative politics of those towns. Wichita State University's IKE Lab found a significant jump in September voter registrations in counties where the ICE raids took place, researcher and professor Alexandra Middlewood said. VOTER REGISTRATIONS RISE Oscar Soto, a grocery store owner in Dodge City, was shocked when he began seeing social media reports of ICE agents flooding his town on September 22. He joined with a group of community organizers to take meals to families afraid to leave home or whose providers had been arrested. He said what he saw that week as he volunteered inspired him to register to vote for the first time at the age of 39. “What can I do to help make any difference at all?" he said he asked himself. "And the one thing I landed on was voting." He said he planned to vote for the Democrat. In the 2024 election, Trump won nearly half the Hispanic vote, but an October 5 Reuters/Ipsos poll showed [USN:L6N45R10Y TEXT:"just 24%"] of Hispanic Americans now approve of Trump's performance in the White House. Hispanic voters made up more than 9% of Kansas voters in 2024, according to the Pew Research Center. CAMPAIGNS TRADE ATTACKS Marshall's campaign has criticized Hamilton over an incident in which a volunteer at a camp connected to his church was accused of molesting two teenage boys. Church leaders initially only investigated the incident internally, later reporting it to police when the volunteer returned to the camp and was again accused of inappropriate behavior. Hamilton has since said the church should have gone to police first and that it changed its policy after the incident to require that. Hamilton’s campaign, in turn, has highlighted a September New York Times report that Marshall, an obstetrician before entering politics, sued more than 700 patients over unpaid medical bills. Marshall said he had followed typical collection practices. Marshall’s campaign did not respond to a request for an interview but issued a statement that said in part he had delivered for farmers, cut middle-class taxes and secured the border, and sought to tie Hamilton to national Democrats, calling him a “Chuck Schumer-funded Democrat,” referring to the Senate minority leader from New York. In Garden City on October 9, a group of voters awaited Hamilton’s visit in a small café, including Michael Shull, a retired pediatrician and registered Republican. Shull said he supported Hamilton because of his moderate political stances and because “he’s willing to talk to people.” Speaking to Reuters after the event, Hamilton zeroed in on the message sent by voters like Shull in reliably Republican Kansas. “It’s not just that Kansas is in play, and we might flip a seat,” Hamilton said. “It’s that people in a reliably red state are saying what’s happening in Washington, DC, is not OK.”

item.title: German regulator fines Nomura over Commerzbank disclosure breaches
item.description: German financial regulator Bafin said on Tuesday it had fined Japanese investment firm Nomura Holdings €320,000 ($359,000) for failing to disclose voting rights in Commerzbank as UniCredit built its stake in the German lender.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: German financial regulator Bafin said on Tuesday it had fined Japanese investment firm Nomura Holdings (8604.T) €320,000 ($359,000) for failing to disclose voting rights in Commerzbank (CBKG.DE) as UniCredit (CRDI.MI) built its stake in the German lender. The regulator said Nomura did not submit voting rights notifications relating to Commerzbank in May and June Under German law, shareholders must notify the issuer and the regulator within four trading days if their voting rights reach certain thresholds If a shareholder does not comply, Bafin can impose a fine of up to €10 million or 5% of total revenue "Whilst we do not comment on the details of our interactions with regulators, the firm takes adherence to regulations seriously," a Nomura spokesperson told Reuters The company can appeal the administrative fine order, Bafin said ($1 = 0.8916 euros)

item.title: US envoy Witkoff to meet Russians, Trump presses Kyiv to settle
item.description: US special envoy Steve Witkoff will travel to Russia on Wednesday after meeting in Oslo with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy and leaders of Norway and Finland, while President Donald Trump said it was time for Kyiv to end the war with Moscow.
item.dc:creator: Nerijus Adomaitis, Lina Golovnya, Steve Holland
item.content:encoded: US special envoy Steve Witkoff will travel to Russia on Wednesday after meeting in Oslo with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy and leaders of Norway and Finland, while President Donald Trump said it was time for Kyiv to end the war with Moscow. Zelenskiy travelled to Oslo in a bid to repair relations with Washington, which have sunk to new lows as Trump has courted Moscow. Kyiv has complained that Washington has withheld vital military support and intelligence. Earlier on Tuesday, Zelenskiy spoke by phone with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Zelenskiy said Ukraine was again receiving early warnings of Russian missile attacks. "Now it works, it's great," he said, adding he and Rubio had also discussed supplies of Patriot missile interceptors and the US-provided satellite-based Starlink system, which Kyiv complained had stopped working when mounted on fast-moving objects such as drones. Trump's recent gestures toward Moscow, including a deal to buy Russian diesel and waiving new sanctions, have sparked bipartisan pushback in the US Congress and worry in European capitals. Zelenskiy said he expected to talk to Rubio again in 48 hours. He said he had discussed security guarantees for Ukraine in Oslo, including "Article 5-like" guarantees, referring to the NATO stipulation that an attack on one ally is an attack on all. "I am thankful to the American side that they underlined again that it will be strong," he said. "There are different kinds of security guarantees which are in the paper, in the document, which Steve (Witkoff) will share with the Russians," he said. "And we will hear his feedback one day after." Zelenskiy reiterated that Ukraine hoped to discuss key issues on how to end the war during a trilateral meeting of leaders of Ukraine, Russia and the US. Norway's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Stoere said the Oslo meeting had been good and constructive. "Steve Witkoff will fly tomorrow to Saint Petersburg where he will be meeting with Russian leadership, and exchange ideas from this meeting and the proposals that have been worked on by European and American colleagues, and possibly pave the way for a meeting at leaders level," Stoere said. "I think the (peace) process is back on track," Finnish President Alexander Stubb told the news conference, in which Witkoff did not take part. Earlier the US envoy and Zelenskiy clasped one another in a hug as they went into the talks that Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner joined remotely. Washington has denied deliberately hindering Ukraine's war effort. But Trump, who has waived sanctions on Russia in what he says is an effort to lower US fuel prices, has repeatedly [USN:L6N4611D3 TEXT:"rebuked Zelenskiy"], and called for him to be [USN:L6N45W06G TEXT:"replaced"]. On Tuesday, Trump called on Ukraine to make a deal to settle the war with Russia, and said Moscow wanted to get it done. "Ukraine has to want to settle this war," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. Trump suggested Moscow had the upper hand in the fight because "Russia is a big machine — they just keep grinding forward, and that's what they've done. They've taken a very large piece of land." On Monday, Trump said Zelenskiy, who has rejected Russia's conditions for ending its war, was "not helping matters much", and that Kyiv should find "somebody else to negotiate". RUBIO SAYS US MISSILES MAY NOT HAVE BEEN DELIVERED YET The US under Trump has largely stopped providing weapons directly to Ukraine but lets European countries buy US weaponry on Kyiv's behalf under the so-called Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL). It has also provided intelligence and technology that Europe cannot match. A source familiar with the matter said most weapons deliveries under PURL continued to flow, but US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has not approved Ukraine’s latest requests for Patriot interceptors. Rubio acknowledged on Tuesday that a consignment of interceptors bought by European countries for Ukraine may not have been delivered, but denied that the US had changed policy. "There has not been some deliberate political directive to go out and harm Ukraine," he said on a visit to India. The Kremlin said it was hoping to set up a meeting between Witkoff and Russian President Vladimir Putin. As US ties with Ukraine have deteriorated, Russia has stepped up attacks on Ukrainian cities, particularly targeting power stations and fuel, despite a call from Trump for both sides to spare each other's energy systems. Russia bombarded cities in western Ukraine overnight, targeting electricity systems and [USN:L1N4660DM TEXT:"knocking out power"] across swathes of the country that had previously been spared. Ukraine held back for several days last week from hitting Russian oil refineries in deference to Trump's request, but has resumed strikes after Russia showed no sign of complying. Both sides have also struck data centres. Trump has repeatedly condemned Ukrainian attacks on Russia while saying little about Russia's far more severe attacks on Ukraine, which have grown even more deadly as Kyiv says US support has been withheld for its air defences. RUSSIAN ATTACKS Russia's defence ministry said on Tuesday it struck three cargo vessels in Ukraine's port of Reni and two other cargo vessels en route to Odesa. Russian forces also hit two logistics hubs, it said. Energy facilities were attacked in seven Ukrainian regions overnight, knocking out power, and the western Lviv region was struck again during the day. Russian drones also struck an energy facility in Kyiv on Tuesday, mayor Vitali Klitschko said, with authorities saying power was out in four districts. The deterioration of US-Ukraine relations began 10 days ago when Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel in a deal agreed with Putin. Trump said this would help reduce high fuel prices that have upset US voters ahead of midterm legislative elections on November 3. At the weekend, Trump issued a broad waiver for tougher sanctions on Russia that were meant to have begun this week.

item.title: Takeaways: Key findings from our investigation of supersized heat waves
item.description: Reuters conducted a data-driven examination of global temperatures that shows heat waves have surged in size and frequency since the 1960s. These are the key takeaways.
item.dc:creator: Maurice Tamman
item.content:encoded: Heat waves have evolved from sporadic, isolated episodes to massive, cascading weather events that blanket vast swaths of the planet for months or even years at a time. To continue calling such sprawling phenomena “heat waves” would be like calling a monsoon a rain shower. To understand the new reality of these immense expanses of heat, Reuters consulted with two dozen climate researchers and analyzed temperatures around the globe for every hour of every day since 1960. From those results, we developed a new concept: the “heat storm.” Scientists and researchers often discuss global warming in the context of risks that will arise if the planet’s average global temperature rises more than 2°C (3.6°F) above pre-industrial levels. What is an ordinary person to make of that? Not much. Heat waves are the connective tissue between the science of global warming and our everyday experience. But supersized heat waves used to be rare. No longer. Now they swarm the planet. Naming events is “a powerful way for people to understand that something is happening,” Anthony Leiserowitz, director of the Yale Program on Climate Change Communication, told Reuters. Yet “we don't currently do that with heat waves,” he said, even though heat has been estimated to kill almost half a million people a year. Read more at https://www.reuters.com/investigates/special-report/climate-heatstorms-takeaways/
