item.title: Thigh injury ends Swiatek's season and WTA Finals bid
item.description: Iga Swiatek ended her season on Tuesday after withdrawing from the Ningbo Open with a thigh injury, a decision that also ended the six-time Grand Slam champion's hopes of qualifying for the WTA Finals.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Iga Swiatek ended her season on Tuesday after withdrawing from the Ningbo Open with a thigh injury, a decision that also ended the six-time Grand Slam champion's hopes of qualifying for the WTA Finals. The 25-year-old Pole, who described the campaign as the most demanding of her career, finished the year without a Grand Slam title. Her last major triumph came at last year's Wimbledon. Swiatek, who has played at every edition of the WTA Finals since 2021 and won the season-ending championships in 2023, needed to reach at least the quarter-finals in Ningbo to have any chance of displacing Czech Karolina Muchova from the last qualifying spot. "After careful consideration, I've decided to withdraw from the tournament," Swiatek said in a statement posted on the Ningbo Open's social media. "I've been experiencing an ongoing problem with my left thigh over the past weeks and I feel that giving myself the time to rest and recover is the right decision." The injury also troubled Swiatek during her [USN:L6N46303P TEXT:"7-5 6-1"] semi-final defeat by compatriot Maja Chwalinska at last week's Wuhan Open. Swiatek finishes the season with a 39-15 record and one title, at the Canadian Open. She also failed to progress beyond the quarter-finals at any of the four Grand Slams. "This has been one of the most demanding seasons of my career, with a lot of challenges, changes and lessons along the way," Swiatek said on social media. "I'm especially proud of the work we've done in the second half of the year and the progress that came with it. It gives me a lot of confidence in what's ahead. "The past few months, or actually the past couple of years, have been incredibly intense and I feel I need to rest and recover my body fully. So that's exactly what I will do, a bit longer this time. I've decided to end my season here, which means I won't be playing any more tournaments this year... "As always, I'll come back with passion and motivation to keep improving..." The former world number one, who has slipped to ninth in the rankings, served a short suspension in late 2024 after an inadvertent doping violation linked to contaminated melatonin, a sleep medication.

item.title: Brazil’s love affair with cellphones turns theft into an election flashpoint
item.description: Brazilian content creator Tabata Lenk had just been fired from her job in Sao Paulo, and was sitting in traffic, when two motorcycle assailants smashed her car window and snatched her brand new cellphone from the dashboard.
item.dc:creator: Andre Romani, Luciana Novaes Magalhaes, Victoria Pachecho
item.content:encoded: Brazilian content creator Tabata Lenk had just been fired from her job in Sao Paulo, and was sitting in traffic, when two motorcycle assailants smashed her car window and snatched her brand new cellphone from the dashboard. Footage of the late-August robbery, recorded on her dashcam, immediately went viral, Lenk said. The reaction points to how an urban nuisance has become one of the defining issues of this year's presidential election. Although phone thefts have been falling since 2023, there were still some 830,000 registered last year, according to the Brazilian Public Security Forum. With Brazil's homicide rate falling by 40% over the last 10 years, to 15.4 per 100,000 people in 2025, according to the Forum, cellphone theft serves as a reminder of how far the country still has to go in bringing a sense of security to its over 210 million people. Cellphone theft still ranks as Brazilians' No. 4 safety concern, a March survey showed, ahead of stray bullets and burglaries. President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and his right-wing challenger Flavio Bolsonaro, who will face off in a tight presidential run-off vote next Sunday, have both been jockeying to show they are tough on phone thieves. Incumbent Lula signed a law earlier this year raising sentences for stolen electronics to up to 10 years in prison and launched a platform to register devices and report thefts, while Bolsonaro has proposed a minimum eight-year prison sentence. "I only want to take aim at the thief and the store that buys and sells the (stolen) phone, I don't want to harm the innocent person who bought it out of necessity," Lula said in a televised address. "The cellphone thief is going to jail," Bolsonaro said in a livestream after the first-round vote. Lenk said she felt so unsafe after the robbery that she only returned to driving alone after getting her windows tinted. "No one should be afraid to leave their house, walk in the street, or use their own cellphone," Lenk said. "So, I believe choosing politicians committed to public safety is essential." BRAZILIANS LOVE THEIR PHONES In one of the world's most online countries, where social media and e-payments dominate daily life, the cellphone has become an indispensable piece of kit. Natasha Bachini Pereira, a researcher at the University of Sao Paulo's Center for the Study of Violence, said the prevalence of cellphone theft explained its political impact. "It's far more common for someone to know of, or have been exposed to, a case of cellphone theft than a car theft, a homicide, or a kidnapping," Pereira said. Phones are expensive in Brazil, and so is replacing them. Research from Deutsche Bank found tariffs, taxes, and currency weakness mean Brazil has the world's second-most expensive iPhone 17 Pro — with a new one retailing at around $2,260, compared with $1,181 in the United States. Even more modest phones represent a huge outlay for many Brazilians. An average cellphone retailed for around 2,310 reais ($456.83) in 2025, according to market data firm IDC, which is about two-thirds of Brazil's average monthly income. Thieves are often just as interested in accessing online banking as the device itself. As digital financial services have expanded rapidly in Brazil – driven by the central bank's Pix payment system – fraud involving stolen devices has exploded, more than quadrupling from 2024 to 2025, according to the Forum, a non-profit to promote public safety policies. After criminals stole Lenk's phone, they took 2,000 reais from her bank account, using Pix. "It's terrible to experience the violence of having your cellphone stolen, but realizing that someone invaded your privacy and managed to steal money from your account is downright agonizing," Lenk said. RECOVERY EFFORTS As Brazil's most populous state, Sao Paulo accounts for almost a third of all phone thefts nationwide, the Brazilian Public Security Forum says, with 268,184 nabbed last year, citing data from state authorities. Police across Sao Paulo are working to prevent phone theft "in the strongest possible way and improve public safety," said Rodolfo Latif Sebba, a civil police chief who is coordinating efforts to find stolen phones. Still, just a fraction of stolen devices are returned to their rightful owners. Between June 2025 and September 23 this year, police in Sao Paulo state recovered 38,028 cellphones and returned 11,445 devices to theft victims, the police said. Student Natalia Eduarda Benvindo, 17, could not believe it when police found her stolen phone. "I asked, 'are you joking?'" Benvindo said. "I couldn't even believe it at the time, wow! I was really happy." (This story has been refiled to fix grammatical errors in paragraph 2.)

item.title: As weight-loss drug users turn to dietary supplements, doctors and regulators raise flags
item.description: For Allison Vecchio, 42, GLP-1 drugs were "a reset button on life," but at a price — side effects like gastrointestinal distress, brittle nails, and feelings of weakness so intense that at times she could not leave her bed.
item.dc:creator: Nicholas Brown
item.content:encoded: For Allison Vecchio, 42, GLP-1 drugs were "a reset button on life," but at a price — side effects like gastrointestinal distress, brittle nails, and feelings of weakness so intense that at times she could not leave her bed. But the Fort Pierce, Florida-based ER nurse said the symptoms eased when she began a cocktail of supplements that included fiber, collagen and electrolytes, a haul that costs $200 to $300 a month. "You really have to take the reins" to turn mere weight loss into improved health, she said. GLP-1 drugs like Novo Nordisk's (NOVOb.CO) Ozempic and Wegovy rank among the biggest medical breakthroughs in years, owing to their efficacy in treating obesity and type 2 diabetes, and reducing the risk of heart disease. Some 10 million Americans used them last year, a figure that could grow to 25 million by 2030, according to JPMorgan research. Their side effects, though, have caused many to turn to loosely regulated dietary supplements. US supplement sales have surged in recent years, surpassing $74 billion in 2025, according to the Nutrition Business Journal. While users swear by them, their growing popularity — fueled in part by social media — has doctors raising red flags and regulators considering new rules around how these products come to market. Vitamins and supplements don't need preapproval by the US Food and Drug Administration, making their scientific credibility hard to gauge. With social media personalities playing a growing role in their promotion, some medical researchers have called for more regulation of online supplement marketing. Rob Fried, CEO of Niagen Bioscience (NAGE.O) , which had $129 million in sales last year, cautioned that companies "can hire an influencer, or even hundreds of influencers on TikTok ... to make whatever claims will sell." SALES OF SUPPLEMENTS SOAR Vecchio has 25,000 TikTok followers and is on retainer with three brands. She is also a member of TikTok Shop's HealthPro creator program, which is reserved for licensed health professionals. Pittsburg, Kansas, resident Terri Hart, 52 — a TikToker with more than 12,000 followers — mostly works on commission, perusing products the brands make available to influencers, and promoting the ones she feels helped her the most. Hart takes magnesium, electrolytes, B12 and other supplements, which she says have helped offset what she called "horrible" nausea, fatigue and constipation after beginning GLP-1s in 2023. They run about $110 a month, costs insurance doesn't cover. TikTok income eases the burden, Hart says. She says she makes clear she isn't a medical professional, and urges followers to talk to doctors before taking her advice. "I establish my authority through my lived experience," Hart said. TikTok Shop generated more than $1 billion in dietary supplement sales in 2025, or 5.4% of all e-commerce supplement sales, according to the Nutrition Business Journal, while overall US vitamin and supplement sales grew 5% in 2024 and 7% last year. The drugs are "bringing in new consumers and expanding existing supplement routines," said Erika Craft, a data analyst at Nutrition Business Journal. But absent FDA preapproval, people don't know exactly what is in many supplements, said Jonathan Bonnet, a clinical associate professor at Stanford and chief medical officer at the Ardmore Institute of Health in Ardmore, Oklahoma. "If you can't know what you're taking, it's hard to know what risks you're undergoing," he said. RETAILERS OFFER MORE SUPPLEMENTS Nearly half of GLP-1 users started taking new vitamins and supplements after beginning the drugs, according to a Nutrition Business Journal survey, with probiotics, protein and fiber particularly popular. A consumer survey by Boston Consulting Group this year said GLP-1 users spend roughly 20% more on protein, fiber and collagen, a protein that helps maintain skin structure, than before starting the drugs. Companies are capitalizing. Target (TGT.N) is widening its supplement offerings, while private equity-owned The Vitamin Shoppe has seen double-digit sales growth this year in fiber and creatine, which are both popular with GLP-1 users, said Jack Gayton, senior vice president of merchandising at The Vitamin Shoppe. Mergers and acquisitions in the space are getting bigger, though with fewer transactions. In 2024, there were 115 deals globally worth $7.3 billion, according to financial data firm PitchBook. In 2025, there were 95 deals worth $16.9 billion. Through October 6 of this year, there have been 68 deals worth $14.6 billion. Procter & Gamble (PG.N) is [USN:L4N4411L4 TEXT:"set to acquire"] supplement maker Thorne, while Japan's Kirin Holdings announced in August it will buy Canada's Jamieson Wellness (JWEL.TO) , whose US-based brand youtheory released a product aimed at GLP-1 users in early 2025. Jamieson spokesperson Ruth Winker said the company sees GLP-1s as a tailwind for growth beyond combating side effects. "As people get healthier, they tend to take more vitamins and supplements," Winker said. REGULATIONS IN THE OFFING US Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has proposed tighter regulations. The FDA this year has stepped up efforts to strengthen oversight of new dietary ingredients, issuing new guidance on what submissions for review should include. Many supplement makers avoid this review process by using a pathway that allows food companies to declare ingredients “generally recognized as safe" without notifying the FDA. But a proposed rule would eliminate that option as part of Kennedy's broader effort to regulate food ingredients. The proposal has divided the industry. Some support more regulation, lamenting unscrupulous actors who spike supplements with drugs or add only tiny amounts of touted beneficial ingredients. “At a minimum, a review process should happen prior to launch," says Jacqueline Maslan, CEO of Body of Work, a vitamin startup aimed at women under 40. But supplement trade group the Council for Responsible Nutrition says the rule would cause months of backlogs as the FDA reviews thousands of ingredients. Thorne CEO Colin Watts said it's “improbable” the FDA could have the manpower to review new ingredients “at the speed needed to keep up with innovation." In a statement to Reuters, an HHS spokesperson said the FDA is mulling opportunities "to modernize its regulatory approach to keep pace with an evolving marketplace," adding the agency wants to ensure product safety "while supporting consumer choice."

item.title: USA-Le Boeing 737 MAX 10 reçoit une certification de la FAA attendue de longue date
item.description: L'administration américaine de l'aviation civile (FAA) a déclaré mardi avoir donné son approbation définitive au 737 MAX 10 de Boeing , au terme d'un processus jalonné de retards, une mesure qui ouvre la voie aux premières livraisons du plus imposant modèle de la gamme 737 de l'avionneur.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: L'administration américaine de l'aviation civile (FAA) a déclaré mardi avoir donné son approbation définitive au 737 MAX 10 de Boeing (BA.N) , au terme d'un processus jalonné de retards, une mesure qui ouvre la voie aux premières livraisons du plus imposant modèle de la gamme 737 de l'avionneur. Cette annonce intervient alors que le secrétaire américain aux Transports, Sean Duffy, devait effectuer dans la journée une visite de l'usine Boeing à Everett, dans l'Etat de Washington, où l'avionneur a ouvert en juillet dernier une nouvelle ligne de production destinée à accroître la fabrication des 737 MAX. Près de 1.500 appareils 737 MAX 10 ont déjà été commandés par diverses compagnies aériennes. Ce modèle représente environ 30% des retards du carnet de commandes de Boeing pour l'ensemble des 737. Un nombre restreints de MAX 10 sont prêts à être livrés. Le processus de certification des avions de Boeing a été renforcé à la suite de deux accidents meurtriers impliquant des MAX 8 en 2018 et 2019, en plus de doutes sur la qualité de certains systèmes de production. La FAA a approuvé en août dernier le 737 MAX 7 au terme d'une procédure ayant duré plus de huit ans. Boeing avait initialement prévu de commencer à livrer le MAX 10 en 2020.

item.title: Sudanese drone attack killed more than 150 people in Abyei market, official says
item.description: South Sudanese officials said Sudan's military had carried out drone strikes that hit a market in the disputed Abyei region, killing more than 150 people, the latest in a series of strikes in one of the bloodiest weeks of a war that has spilled across Sudan's borders.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: South Sudanese officials said Sudan's military had carried out drone strikes that hit a market in the disputed Abyei region, killing more than 150 people, the latest in a series of strikes in one of the bloodiest weeks of a war that has spilled across Sudan's borders. The strike pushed the toll from attacks in recent days to more than 250, underscoring the lethality of airstrikes in [USN:L6N40Y0KB TEXT:"Sudan's war"], which erupted in April 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), triggering a major humanitarian crisis and drawing in local militias and foreign powers. Yohana Akol Ngor, the caretaker minister of information in Abyei, told Reuters on Tuesday that the death toll from the attack on the market in Abyei on Monday had jumped to 153 from 73, but was likely to rise further. "The fire is still burning. So the recovery process of the dead ones is still continuing. The situation is terrible," Ngor said, adding that some bodies had been burned to ashes. A video filmed at the scene on Tuesday and verified by Reuters showed the charred and twisted remains of vehicles and buildings. Flames still billowed from one building as residents inspected the damage. He said Sudan's army was responsible for the attack, without providing evidence. A spokesperson for Sudan's armed forces did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Three diplomatic sources, an aid worker and an expert on the conflict told Reuters the strike hit a fuel depot in the market. The diplomatic sources said the depot had been used in the past by the RSF to supply its forces. A spokesperson for the RSF did not immediately respond to requests for comment. OIL-RICH ABYEI South Sudan declared independence from Sudan in 2011. Since then, both countries have staked a claim to oil-rich Abyei, which is jointly administered. It borders Sudan's Kordofan region, which has become a major centre of fighting in the war. Officials in Sudan's military-led government told Reuters the RSF is active in parts of Abyei. Ngor denied the presence of the RSF in Abyei. Reuters could not immediately verify the claims. The United Nations Interim Security Force for Abyei (UNISFA) warned in May that the presence of the RSF in Abyei had increased insecurity there, adding that delays in determining the disputed region's final status had put civilians and UNISFA personnel at risk. UN spokesperson Stephane Dujarric said the UN strongly condemned the series of drone attacks in Abyei and other areas. "We remain alarmed by the relentless drone attacks across Sudan, as well as the damage they are causing to critical infrastructure - these attacks are taking a devastating toll on communities already struggling with the consequences of more than three years of conflict," Dujarric told reporters in New York. STRUGGLE TO RETRIEVE BODIES Ngor told Reuters that emergency workers had struggled to retrieve the bodies because of fires caused by the strikes. Some 8,000 people had been displaced by Monday's bombing, Ngor added. South Sudan's foreign ministry said late on Monday that drones struck a market located north of Abyei town, but did not specify the number of civilian casualties or provide a toll. The ministry said it had summoned the Sudanese ambassador in protest. An eyewitness said he heard five large explosions that led to the fuel market catching fire. "People started evacuating the casualties. They had injuries from shrapnel on their stomach and legs ... In one site, I saw 28 bodies that were burnt," the witness said, asking not to be named for safety reasons. The witness said they did not see any sign of RSF or other uniformed fighters in the market, where goods like sugar, flour and biscuits are also sold for shipment into Sudan. DEADLY WEEK Sudanese armed forces and the RSF have recently escalated [USN:L6N44V0K3 TEXT:"drone strikes"], with a series of attacks targeting RSF-held Nyala and army-held Khartoum airport this week. On Sunday, drone attacks in West Kordofan state in Sudan, controlled by the RSF, killed some 84 people and injured 65 others, according to the local Emergency Response Room. On Monday, four children were killed after repeated drone attacks targeted SAF-controlled Khartoum airport. On Friday, an attack on a market in RSF stronghold Nyala killed 23 people and injured 44, according to volunteers there. Chadian authorities have accused Sudan’s military of carrying out drone strikes on its territory, which UN experts say is regularly used by RSF supply lines. Sudan's foreign ministry said in late August that its armed forces were acting to protect the country's security. On October 10, [USN:L1N45X06E TEXT:"an airstrike"] close to Sudan's border with Egypt killed more than 70 artisanal miners, according to a local rights group. PATIENTS TREATED FOR BURNS Abyei experiences frequent bouts of violence, with clashes usually involving rival ethnic groups or armed militias. The attack is the deadliest in years to hit the area, where medical supplies and healthcare are scarce. South Sudan's government says it has not taken sides in its neighbour's war. However, diplomats and experts say Abyei has established itself as crucial, serving as a transit point for RSF logistics, particularly fuel. Medical charity Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF) said it was treating more than 20 wounded, some with burns, at the nearby Ameth Bek Hospital. "We are providing surgical services and wound dressing, along with other emergency care," said Christian Lindauer, MSF medical activities manager at the facility. Photographs shared on MSF's official social media account showed bandaged patients lying on the floor as they received care for their injuries.

item.title: Gold edges lower as investors weigh Fed rate signals
item.description: Gold edged lower on Tuesday as investors weighed the likelihood of additional US interest rate hikes this year ahead of next week's Federal Reserve policy meeting.
item.dc:creator: Anushree Mukherjee
item.content:encoded: Gold edged lower on Tuesday as investors weighed the likelihood of additional US interest rate hikes this year ahead of next week's Federal Reserve policy meeting. Spot gold was down 0.3% at $4,125.90 per ounce by 02:05 p.m. EDT (1805 GMT). US gold futures for December delivery settled 0.4% lower at $4,142.60 per ounce. "Inflation and the Fed's interest rates are the big stories that gold's fighting at the moment. US Treasuries do appear more favorable than gold as a safety asset for the moment," said Bob Haberkorn, senior market strategist at StoneX. "$4,000 is a big level for (gold) to keep an eye on and see if it can hold. A lot of that, at the moment, is going to be dependent on what the Fed says," Haberkorn said. The Fed raised interest rates by a quarter point in September, its first hike this year. While recent comments from [USN:L6N462084 TEXT:"Fed"] officials signaling little [USN:L1N4600EO TEXT:"urgency"] for further policy tightening have tempered expectations of a rate hike at the central bank's October 27-28 policy meeting, traders see a 92% chance of a hike in December, according to CME's FedWatch Tool . FEDWATCH Gold is still down about 26% from its record high of $5,594.82 in January and roughly 22% from levels at the start of the Iran war , when concerns over energy inflation reinforced bets on interest rate hikes. Gold is traditionally seen as an inflation hedge, but it loses its appeal as a non-yielding asset in a high-interest-rate environment. Investors are also watching next week's US Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) data, the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge, for clues on whether inflation pressures remain persistent and how that could shape the rate outlook. In Japan, central bank Governor Kazuo Ueda [USN:L1N465004 TEXT:"said"] underlying inflation was "quite close" to the 2% target, signaling scope for further rate hikes. Among other metals, spot silver rose 1.4% to $57.86 per ounce, platinum gained 1% to $1,656.85 per ounce and palladium dropped 1.3% to $1,105.50 per ounce.

item.title: Dollar dips as traders weigh Iran, AI risks
item.description: The US dollar slipped on Tuesday in line with falling oil prices and longer-dated Treasury yields as traders evaluated the impact of rising tensions in the US war with Iran and the durability of strong capital inflows into US AI companies.
item.dc:creator: Karen Brettell
item.content:encoded: The US dollar slipped on Tuesday in line with falling oil prices and longer-dated Treasury yields as traders evaluated the impact of rising tensions in the US war with Iran and the durability of strong capital inflows into US AI companies. Oil prices slipped after touching a [USN:L1N46601X TEXT:"five-month high"] as traders weighed a meeting between the Iranian president and Pakistan's army chief, a key US-Iran mediator, against continued Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure and reports of vessel attacks in the Gulf. Higher oil prices have raised concern about inflation staying higher for longer. The dollar jumped last week after data showed that US consumer price inflation [USN:L1N45Z121 TEXT:"accelerated in September"]. But that move was soon overtaken by concerns over AI. "Energy prices pushing higher is good for the dollar, but if it gets to the point where rates go so high that the AI trade blows up, suddenly it has a negative impact," said Dominic Bunning, head of G10 FX strategy at Nomura. "There's a threshold there and we're playing around with that at the moment." Strong capital inflows into AI stocks in the US have supported the dollar. Higher interest rates, driven partly by growth and inflation expectations tied to the sector, have helped. But concerns over AI were renewed earlier on Tuesday as shares in South Korean AI services firm Elice Group (0158S0.KQ) plunged 32% in their Seoul [USN:L1N46600F TEXT:"market debut"]. The dollar index , which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies including the yen and the euro, fell 0.25% to 101.71, with the euro up 0.22% at $1.1235. Traders remained wary of the euro despite Tuesday's gains as France faces widespread protests and a worsening fiscal picture. France will reinforce police with troops and mount a huge security operation for [USN:L6N4660DJ TEXT:"more protests"] planned on Saturday, the government said on Tuesday, acknowledging failures in its response to last weekend's violence. "The worries in France are not going away anytime soon," said Tommy von Brömsen, FX strategist at Handelsbanken. "The bearish view on France will stay for a while longer, and there's much more euro weakness to be priced in." Britain's pound strengthened 0.59% to $1.338 after labour market data showed a resilient [USN:L8N46608R TEXT:"jobs market"], the latest batch of data from the UK that surprised to the upside. "The risk is that a resilient labour market gives the Bank of England both the room and the reason to raise interest rates again," said Lale Akoner, global market strategist at eToro. "Sterling could benefit from rising rate expectations." Markets are almost fully pricing in a 25-basis-point rate hike by the Bank of England at its next meeting on November 5, according to LSEG data. STRONG JAPANESE BOND AUCTION The yen jumped after an auction of longer-dated Japanese government bonds (JGBs) drew [USN:L1N46604J TEXT:"record demand"]. "The record 20-year auction is a strong signal that sidelined cash is finally coming back," said Masahiko Loo, senior fixed-income strategist at State Street Investment Management in Tokyo. "JGBs are also starting to look like a relative haven from Europe's political and fiscal volatility, particularly around France." The Japanese yen gained 0.21% to 158.14 per dollar. Elsewhere, the Canadian dollar rose 0.34% to 1.406 per US dollar, its strongest level in almost a month, after Alberta residents voted by a [USN:L6N4651AT TEXT:"large majority"] to remain part of Canada in the province's first-ever referendum on separation.

item.title: Brent falls as Iran's president discusses mediation with Pakistani army chief
item.description: Oil prices settled down after touching a five-month high on Tuesday as traders weighed a meeting between the Iranian president and Pakistan's army chief, a key US-Iran mediator, against continued Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure and reports of vessel attacks in the Gulf.
item.dc:creator: Georgina Mccartney
item.content:encoded: Oil prices settled down after touching a five-month high on Tuesday as traders weighed a meeting between the Iranian president and Pakistan's army chief, a key US-Iran mediator, against continued Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure and reports of vessel attacks in the Gulf. Brent crude futures settled down 76 cents, or 0.69%, at $108.79. Earlier in the session, the front-month contract reached $111.99, a five-month high. The November contract for US West Texas Intermediate crude, which expired on Tuesday, settled down $1.87, or 1.8%, at $101.79. That was down from the session high of $110.48, the highest since April for a nearby contract. The more active December contract settled down 72 cents at $97.82 a barrel. Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian discussed [USN:S8N455017 TEXT:"mediation efforts"] and regional developments during a meeting with Pakistan's army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir in Tehran, Iran's Nournews reported on Tuesday. Pakistan's mediation efforts resulted in an interim peace agreement signed in June. But that deal quickly faltered amid new fighting between Iran and the US weeks later. The talks in Tehran are against the backdrop of continued attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis, who said on Monday they launched [USN:S8N44M08Y TEXT:"several attacks"] on Saudi energy, airport and military targets, such as an Aramco (2222.SE) site in Yanbu, the Shaybah oilfield, Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport and Abha airport. Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm the Houthi claims and Reuters could not independently verify them. "Oil prices remain well-supported... This suggests the market is pricing in a significant risk premium, given the situation's volatility," ING analysts said in a note on Tuesday. At least 18 vessels were reportedly attacked over two weeks, which keeps the risk premium intact, shiptracker Kpler said in a note on Monday. Also on Monday, a Houthi [USN:L1N46509O TEXT:"attack"] on a training camp for government security forces in Yemen's Shabwa province killed 58 people and injured more than 200. The renewed attacks heightened fears about regional stability and underscored continuing risks to energy supply from the region, keeping oil prices above $100 a barrel. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin [USN:L8N4661N0 TEXT:"Netanyahu"] said in a statement he is "committed to completing the elimination of the Iranian regime," and spoke with US President Donald Trump about it on Sunday. DIESEL SUPPLY Russian diesel cargoes are returning to their traditional destinations after the [USN:L6N4660Q8 TEXT:"US suspended sanctions"] and secured the lifting of an export ban, with at least two tankers signaling trips to Turkey and Brazil in recent days, according to shipping data from Kpler and LSEG. The US is [USN:L1N4660KS TEXT:"working with domestic refiners"] to squeeze more crude through its refining complex, US Energy Under Secretary Kyle Haustveit said on Tuesday at the Drake Forum in Titusville, Pennsylvania, a sentiment echoed by US Energy Secretary Chris Wright later on Tuesday in Houston. The US is also pushing shuttered domestic refineries to reopen, Wright added. US crude oil stockpiles were expected to have fallen last week along with product inventories, an extended Reuters poll showed on Tuesday. Eight analysts polled by Reuters estimated, on average, that crude inventories fell by about 800,000 barrels in the week ended October 16.

item.title: Alberta votes by large majority to remain part of Canada in boost for Carney
item.description: Alberta residents voted by a large majority to remain part of Canada in the province's first-ever referendum on separation, handing Prime Minister Mark Carney a much-needed win as he attempts to unify the country amid a trade war with the US.
item.dc:creator: Amanda Stephenson, Maria Cheng
item.content:encoded: Alberta residents voted by a large majority to remain part of Canada in the province's first-ever referendum on [USN:L6N3Z2101 TEXT:"separation"], handing Prime Minister Mark Carney a much-needed win as he attempts to unify the country amid a [USN:SPN44J009 TEXT:"trade war"] with the US. At 5:45 a.m. (1145 GMT) on Tuesday, with three-quarters of the votes counted, 76% of Albertans had backed the "remain" side versus 24% in favor of a binding vote on separation. The [USN:L6N46019J TEXT:"referendum"] was nonbinding. "Albertans made a clear choice," Carney said in a statement. "They chose unity, to build together, and to take care of each other." "Canada is greater than the sum of its parts," he said. Pollsters and analysts had dismissed the possibility of a separatist victory in Monday's vote, citing data that showed only about one-third of residents in the western energy-producing province supported a future referendum on leaving. Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, who announced the referendum in May, issued a statement saying she was "very pleased" that early results showed widespread support for remaining in Canada. Smith said she would address Albertans at 6:45 p.m. on Tuesday to discuss "where our province goes from here." A small but vocal group of separatists has campaigned for months for an independent Alberta, arguing that the province's energy wealth was subsidizing poorer parts of Canada and that it would be far richer freed from Ottawa bureaucracy. Last week, Carney told a rally in Calgary that voting to leave Canada would be "a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep division". CARNEY SEEKS TO REDUCE CANADA'S DEPENDENCE ON US There was no immediate reaction to the vote's outcome from President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly talked about the United States annexing Canada. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, discussing Alberta in January, said: "I think we should let them come down into the US." Monday's vote was the second time in two weeks that Carney has had to face a separatist challenge. An independence-minded party won [USN:L1N4590X4 TEXT:"power"] in the predominantly French-speaking province of Quebec on October 5 but fell short of the majority needed to fulfill a vow to hold a vote on breaking with Canada. Quebec held independence referendums in 1980 and 1995, both of which failed. Carney, who grew up mostly in Alberta, acknowledges Albertans have often felt slighted by Ottawa. He has noted his government fast-tracked a proposed [USN:L1N45N0PP TEXT:"new pipeline"], with Alberta and the federal government as majority owners. And he has pointed to Alberta's critical role in helping Canada reduce its dependence on the US. First Nations groups have also [USN:L6N41R10Y TEXT:"objected"] to the idea of an independent Alberta, as their land treaties with Ottawa predate the province's creation within Canada. ALBERTA INDEPENDENCE MOVEMENT SET TO CARRY ON The result is unlikely to end the independence movement. Before the referendum, some separatist leaders said they would continue to pursue another vote even if most Albertans said they wanted to remain. According to data released on October 16 by the pollster Angus Reid, 62% of Albertans believe "there will never be an end to the separatist movement". The vote on Monday also included [USN:L6N3ZF146 TEXT:"nine other nonbinding questions"] on proposed measures to strengthen the province's hand when dealing with Ottawa. These covered immigration, access to provincial services — such as education, social care and healthcare — and voter identification requirements. Provisional results showed voters backed eight of the nine measures, but some with only small majorities.
